opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think people often frame this as a dichotomy: either progress comes from clever new ideas, or it comes from just scaling things up. I don't think that's quite the right way to see it.

Coming from physics, I like to think in terms of what changes and what stays the same as you vary some parameter. Scale is a knob, and a really important one. One of the surprising empirical facts of the last several years is how smoothly and predictably performance improves as you turn it: more compute, more data, bigger models. Scaling laws are about as close as we've gotten in machine learning to something that feels like a physical law. And a lot of the progress people attribute to "AI getting smarter" is really that knob being turned.

But ideas matter in a different way. A good idea changes the slope or the offset of those curves, or it unlocks a new curve you can climb. The transformer is the obvious example: it wasn't just a better model at a fixed size. It was an architecture that scaled better, so it made all the subsequent compute more valuable. The same goes for things like reinforcement learning on top of pretrained models, or getting models to think longer at inference time. That opens up a new axis to scale along.

So the way I'd put it is that ideas and scale are multiplicative, not competing. Scale tells you that if you have something that works, you can make it work a lot better by throwing resources at it. Ideas tell you what's worth throwing resources at. And there's a feedback loop: once you have a lot of compute, the bar for what counts as a good idea shifts. Ideas that don't scale tend to get washed out, and the ones that survive are the ones that compose well with scale. That's the "bitter lesson," in a sense, though I'd say it's less bitter than people make it out to be. It's a lesson about which ideas matter, not a claim that ideas don't matter.

From a theory perspective, part of what I find exciting is trying to understand why scaling works the way it does. If you understand the underlying principles, you can predict which ideas will scale before spending the compute, and that's where theory can feed back into practice.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scale and AI progress but does not say that insufficient scale kept researchers from exploring ideas developed in the 1980s and 1990s.

r002.rationale: It says ideas can change scaling curves, but does not suggest that scaling laws arise from the data process when an architecture has no fundamental defect.

r003.rationale: It says Transformers scaled better, but does not identify their suitability for available training hardware as a reason they could reach large scale.

r004.rationale: It describes ideas as unlocking new curves, but does not explain that removing a scaling bottleneck makes scale seem especially important by enabling results from previously available ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the two are much more entangled than the usual framing suggests. People tend to set it up as a dichotomy: either progress comes from clever new ideas, or it comes from just throwing more compute and data at the same recipe. But if you look at the actual history of the field, almost every important new idea was an idea that let scale work better. The transformer is the obvious example. It wasn't a new theory of intelligence. It was an architecture that happened to be extremely well suited to being parallelized and trained on huge amounts of data, and that's precisely why it won.

So I'd put it this way: scale is the engine, and ideas are what let you keep turning it. Scaling laws tell you something remarkable, which is that if you increase compute in a disciplined way, performance improves in a predictable way. That's a very unusual thing to have in a science, and it's what let the field make long-range bets. But the laws aren't laws of nature in the sense of being eternal. They're empirical regularities for a particular recipe. Every so often you hit a wall, whether that's data, or the cost of inference, or just the fact that you can't buy ten times more GPUs next year, and then you need a new idea to change the exponent, or to find a different axis to scale along. Test-time compute and reinforcement learning on reasoning are a recent version of that. The idea unlocked a new dimension, and then scaling did the rest.

My own background is in theoretical physics, so I'm biased toward wanting to understand why any of this works. And I think that matters practically, not just aesthetically. If you have a theory of why scaling behaves the way it does, you can make better predictions about where the next wall is and what kind of idea might get you past it, instead of just running the experiment and hoping. The people who dismiss scale as brute force are missing that it's been the most reliable source of progress we've ever had. And the people who think it's only scale are missing that someone had to come up with the thing being scaled.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention 1980s or 1990s AI ideas being left unexplored because scale was insufficient.

r002.rationale: It describes scaling laws as empirical regularities for a particular recipe, but does not attribute them to the underlying data process when an architecture has no fundamental defect.

r003.rationale: It says Transformers were well suited to parallelization and large-scale training, but does not identify their fit with available training hardware as the reason they could practically reach that scale.

r004.rationale: It says new ideas can address scaling walls and unlock new axes, but does not explain that removing a bottleneck makes scale appear especially important by enabling results from previously available ideas.

astra-6.text:
I think ideas and scale reinforce each other. A new idea can make it possible to use more compute effectively, and scaling a system can expose limitations that force you to find new ideas. So I’m skeptical of treating them as competing explanations for progress.

The tricky part is that the contribution of an idea isn’t always obvious at small scale. Something might look unremarkable in a small experiment but become important as you scale up. Conversely, a clever approach might give you an immediate improvement without continuing to improve as you put more resources into it.

So the question I’d ask is: does this idea change how much we get out of scale? That’s where the two really meet.

r002.rationale: It says ideas and scale reinforce each other, but does not connect scaling laws to the underlying data process or qualify that claim by an architecture having no fundamental defect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think new ideas and scale are deeply complementary. An idea can make computation more useful, and scale can reveal that an idea works much better than you could have seen in a small experiment.

So I’m skeptical of the framing that progress is either about clever algorithms or just making things bigger. Scaling a system reliably involves a lot of ideas—in architecture, optimization, data, and infrastructure. And once you scale it, you encounter new behavior and new bottlenecks that motivate the next set of ideas.

The interesting question is: what lets us turn additional resources into additional capability? Sometimes that’s a conceptual breakthrough, sometimes it’s an engineering improvement, and often it’s the interaction between the two.
